title: Module 2 Quiz: The Full Quantum Concept

questions.prompt: What does it mean for a qubit to be in superposition?
options: It exists as a combination of 0 and 1 until measured
questions.explanation: Superposition means the qubit holds a combination of both basis states until measured, at which point it collapses to one.

questions.prompt: How many simultaneous states can a system of n qubits represent (ideally, before measurement)?
questions.explanation: n qubits can represent 2^n states simultaneously in superposition, the source of quantum parallelism.

questions.prompt: What happens when two qubits become entangled?
options: They can no longer be measured
Measuring one instantly determines information about the other, regardless of distance
They merge into a single classical bit
questions.explanation: Entanglement links qubits so measuring one gives instant information about the correlated state of the other.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes QKD from PQC?
options: QKD uses quantum physics/hardware to distribute keys; PQC uses classical math on ordinary computers
PQC requires quantum hardware; QKD does not
questions.explanation: QKD distributes keys using quantum phenomena over specialized hardware. PQC is classical math designed to resist quantum attacks and runs on today's computers — Q-CAPS focuses on PQC.

questions.prompt: What best describes today's 'NISQ era' quantum computers?
options: Fully error-corrected machines that can already break RSA-2048
Noisy, intermediate-scale machines not yet capable of breaking modern RSA/ECC at scale
Machines that only run classical algorithms
questions.explanation: NISQ machines are still limited by noise and scale, and cannot yet break RSA-2048 in practice — but proactive migration is still needed.

questions.prompt: In the qubit notation α|0⟩ + β|1⟩, what do α and β represent conceptually?
options: The physical temperature of the qubit
The number of logic gates used
questions.explanation: α and β are probability amplitudes; their squared magnitudes give the probability of measuring 0 or 1 respectively.
